questionText: "I leave the residue of my estate on trust to be divided between such of my living descendants as my trustees in their absolute discretion may decide." Which of the following is the most accurate in relation to this clause? Question Score: 1 / 1
subject: Trusts Law
userAnswer: This is a discretionary trust and the trustees must provide a complete list of all potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
correctAnswer: This is a discretionary trust so the trustees should apply the any given postulant test to the potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.

questionText: Two business partners purchased a freehold shop together five years ago. They contributed equally to the purchase price and both appear on the title as registered proprietors. They initially agreed to hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants. They have received tax advice and now wish to bring the joint tenancy to an end, but wish to remain co-owners. How can the business partners give effect to the tax advice? Question Score: 1 / 1
subject: Land Law
source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: The joint tenancy in law must be severed and a form A restriction placed on the proprietorship register.
correctAnswer: The joint tenancy in equity must be severed and a form A restriction placed on the proprietorship register.

questionText: A defendant has been prosecuted for a non-imprisonable summary offence relating to food standards. The court has adjourned the matter for trial and is considering bail. The defendant has said certain things to the food standards officers during the inspection that cause the magistrates to think that the defendant might commit further offences before trial. In what circumstances can the court refuse bail in this situation? Question Score: 1 / 1
subject: Criminal Law and Practice
source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: Only if the defendant has previously breached bail conditions and the magistrates’ concerns about potential offences are substantial.
correctAnswer: It cannot because the defendant has not been convicted.

questionText: A purchaser wished to buy a painting by a famous and sought-after artist, who was a distant relative. They did not know much about art, but they knew what they liked when they saw it. The purchaser registered their interest with an art dealer who said they had a painting by the artist for sale. The purchaser asked if the painting was genuinely by the artist, making it clear they would not purchase unless it was by their relative. The art dealer took all reasonable steps to verify the painting and confirmed that it was genuine. The purchaser bought the painting for £8,000. Eighteen months ago, the purchaser discovered the painting was a very good forgery and worth about £150. When they bought the painting, works by the artist were selling for £20,000 and the price has remained stable. Ignoring interest, what is the amount of damages the purchaser can claim?
subject: Contract Law

questionText: A group of three set designers work in partnership on projects for TV and film. On their last project, the production company shut down the production and kept some of their equipment and working materials. The designers want to issue a claim against the production company for unpaid fees and damages to compensate them for the loss of their property. The total value of the claim is approximately £70,000. How should the designers issue their claim?
subject: Dispute Resolution
source: DISP8.4: Commencing court proceedings: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: Take or send the claim form to the County Court hearing centre nearest to the registered office of the production company.
correctAnswer: Send a claim form to the CIvil National Business Centre.

questionText: Four friends wish to set up a business in partnership and so enter into a written partnership agreement that specifies:- All of them have contributed an equal amount of capital to the business.- Interest is paid on their capital contributions at 5% pa.- All of them share profits and losses equally.- One of the partners is paid a salary of £10,000 pa.Which statement best reflects the friends’ position under the Partnership Act 1890?
subject: Business Law and Practice
userAnswer: They have excluded the default provisions under the Partnership Act 1890 in relation to the payment of a salary only.
correctAnswer: They have excluded the default provisions under the Partnership Act 1890 in relation to the payment of interest on capital and the payment of a salary.

questionText: An interior designer borrowed £5,000 from their restaurateur cousin to assist in setting up an interior design business. In return, the interior designer agreed to repay the restaurateur as soon as possible and to assist them in redecorating the interior of one of their restaurants. When the restaurant opened there was a lot of favourable publicity, especially with regard to the new décor and business boomed. The interior designer’s business also benefited from being showcased in the restaurant. The interior designer now tells the restaurateur they consider the design work for the restaurant is equivalent to £5,000, so they do not intend to repay the loan. Can the restaurateur recover the money?
subject: Contract Law
userAnswer: Yes, there is a claim because consideration has been provided.
correctAnswer: Yes, there is a claim because this is not a social arrangement.

questionText: An unmarried couple (A and B) are splitting up. The house, which they have lived in as their home, is owned in the sole name of A. B did not contribute to the purchase price of the property. B is worried that A might sell the house and want B to move out. Which of the following statements best describes B’s legal position?
subject: Land Law
source: LAND4.2: Title to land: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: B should register a class F land charge against the title to the property to protect B’s right of occupation.
correctAnswer: B should remain in occupation of the property but does not have an interest that is capable of protection.

questionText: A police officer arrests a suspect, having seen him as a part of a crowd during an affray seemingly engaged in threatening unlawful violence. The suspect is taken to the police station to be detained. What reason could the officer provide to the custody officer for the arrest?
subject: Criminal Law and Practice
source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: They had reasonable grounds to believe that the arrestee has committed an indictable offence.
correctAnswer: They had reasonable grounds to suspect that the arrestee has committed an offence and that they had reasonable grounds for believing the arrest to be necessary.

questionText: During a rally, the defendant fires off a gun. The shot shatters a window and narrowly misses a person standing beyond it. The defendant denies having intended to put anyone’s life at risk claiming instead simply to have been joining in the spirit of the protest. Could the defendant be guilty of aggravated criminal damage?
subject: Criminal Liability
source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: Yes, if the defendant realised that firing the bullet through the window put the person in danger.
correctAnswer: No, because there does not appear to be any recklessness as to endangering life by damage to property.

questionText: A solicitor in a sole practice has been found with a small amount of Class A drugs at a house party. The solicitor has accepted a caution for the offence. Which of the following best describes the professional conduct implications in the circumstances?
subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: The solicitor has not breached any conduct regulations given that the offence is minor and only attracted a caution.
correctAnswer: The solicitor is in breach of the conduct regulations as the solicitor has failed to uphold public trust and confidence in the profession.

questionText: You are an office manager with a background in working for online digital service companies. You started work 3 months ago at a law firm at their Manchester city centre office as their office manager. After a month, the managing partner of the firm asked for money to be transferred from the client account to the business account as a temporary short-term loan to the business. You were worried about the request as it didn’t seem in line with normal business practice, however, you did not object and the transfer took place. The Solicitors Regulatory Authority (SRA) have now announced they are investigating the firm for breaches to the Code of Conduct for Firms, breaches of the Code of Conduct for Solicitors, and breaches of the relevant Principles. Is the office manager bound by any of the Codes or the Principles?
subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
source: COND3.1: Overview of Principles and Codes Part 1: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: Yes, regardless of qualification, the office manager is still bound by the Code of Conduct for Firms.
correctAnswer: Yes, regardless of qualification, the office manager is bound by the Code of Conduct for Firms and the Principles.

questionText: A partnership operates under a written agreement that specifies that the partnership will continue for a fixed period of 5 years. After 3 years have elapsed, one of the partners would like to retire from the partnership. Which statement best reflects the partner’s position?
subject: Business Law and Practice
userAnswer: As it is a fixed term partnership, the partner cannot leave until the fixed period ends.
correctAnswer: The partner cannot leave the partnership during the fixed term without the consent of their fellow partners to vary the agreement to permit retirement.

questionText: A teacher who is unable to drive as they suffer from epilepsy has applied for a job at a private school and was not invited to the second interview. Has the school acted in a discriminatory way?
subject: Legal Services
userAnswer: No, because there is no prohibited conduct, as the school were acting in a proportionate way to achieve a legitimate aim.
correctAnswer: Yes, because this treatment could fall within the definition of prohibited conduct in respect of the teacher's epilepsy.

questionText: A surveyor served a defence relying on comparable sales data and a named estate agent report. Can the claimant obtain clarification and documents at this stage?
subject: Dispute Resolution
userAnswer: They are entitled to copies of the report and documents containing the data relied upon for the valuation.
correctAnswer: They can serve a request for further information and obtain a copy of the report, but not any other documents.

questionText: A painter abandons a decorating contract halfway through after taking a deposit. What is the legal position?
subject: Contract Law
userAnswer: The homeowner is liable to pay the painter on a quantum meruit basis for the work done.
correctAnswer: The homeowner does not have to pay on a quantum meruit basis for the work as it is only partial performance.

questionText: A developer threatens a homeowner ("in a pine box") to sell their house. The homeowner signs. What is the likely outcome in contract?
subject: Contract Law
userAnswer: The resident can elect to have the contract set aside.
correctAnswer: The resident was subject to duress over the sale. The contract is void.

questionText: A software engineer makes offensive comments about a colleague's sexual orientation and posts offensive images. What best explains this behaviour?
subject: Legal Services
userAnswer: The software engineer's behaviour is harassment because the conduct is linked to the administrator's sexual orientation.
correctAnswer: The software engineer's behaviour is harassment because the conduct is linked to the administrator's sexual orientation and affects the administrator's dignity.

questionText: A defendant is unrepresented in a summary trial, in which they rely on an alibi defence. The defendant gives evidence in their own defence and calls two alibi witnesses. The defendant does not know what the position is in relation to closing speeches and asks the court legal advisor for help. How should the court legal advisor respond?
subject: Criminal Law and Practice
source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)
userAnswer: Neither the prosecution nor the defence have the right to make a closing speech because the trial is a summary trial.
correctAnswer: The prosecution and the defence can make closing speeches.

questionText: The carer of an elderly testator is an avid amateur actor and a member of the local amateur dramatic society. The carer visited their client daily and regularly spoke to them about the society and its financial struggles. The testator had never demonstrated any interest in theatre during their life. In their will, after some minor bequests to family, the testator left the residue of their estate on trust for the benefit of the local amateur dramatic society. The carer was one of the witnesses to the will. The testator's family want to challenge the bequest to the dramatic society. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this situation?
subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
correctAnswer: The family will need to demonstrate that the carer's influence was sufficient to amount to coercion or pressure that overpowered the freedom of action of the testator.

questionText: A private limited company is a small family-run business with all of the four shareholders living in the same postcode district. Three of the shareholders each own 30% of shares entitling them to attend and vote at a general meeting. The fourth shareholder owns the remaining 10%. A couple of company matters require an urgent shareholder meeting and they ask your advice on whether they can shorten the notice needed for this meeting. Which of the statements below best describes your advice?
subject: Business Law and Practice
correctAnswer: A majority in number of members owning not less than 90% of the voting shares need to consent to short notice; so the three shareholders who each own 30% of the shares all need to consent.

questionText: A solicitor acts for a client in relation to the acquisition of a private limited company. Two days before the transaction is due to complete, the solicitor suspects that the client will be using the transaction to launder money. The solicitor reports this to the nominated officer who makes a suspicious activity report to the relevant authority. What action should the solicitor now take?
subject: Legal Services
correctAnswer: Proceed with the transaction only after receiving authorisation from the relevant authority.

questionText: The judge at the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) needs to apply the Social Services Act 1988. Section 5 of the Act refers to “family”. When applying the literal rule, the judge is faced with an absurd outcome that does not fit the current case.Which is the next step that the judge needs to take?
subject: Legal System
correctAnswer: The judge should apply the golden rule.

questionText: A Member of Parliament (MP) has recently introduced a private memberʼs bill in the House of Commons.What stages does the Bill need to go through to become law?
subject: Legal System
correctAnswer: The Bill needs to go through three readings and a committee stage at the House of Commons and the House of Lords and then receive the Royal Assent

questionText: A department store ordered boxed chocolates to sell in its store. It was listed as a written term of the contract that the chocolates be packaged in the storeʼs own-brand packaging, as the store famously only sells own- branded products. Once delivered it was discovered that the chocolates were instead in packaging representing the manufacturerʼs brand. The manufacturer claims the packaging detail was only a warranty and the store can still sell the goods. The department store says it was obviously a condition and they cannot sell the goods. What is the likely legal position?
subject: Contract Law
correctAnswer: The clause will be held to be a condition of the contract.

questionText: A grandparent purchased a brand-new car for a grandchild. After 18 months, the grandparent paid to replace the rear nearside tyre, because it had a puncture. Unfortunately, the replacement tyre was defective and caused a blowout on the motorway. The grandchildʼs car collided with the centre reservation and was written off. The grandchild was unharmed. Does the grandchild have a claim in negligence against the manufacturer of the tyre?
subject: Tort
correctAnswer: Yes, but not in respect of the replacement tyre.

questionText: A business that provides wedding venues has been served with a claim form and particulars of claim from a couple who were dissatisfied with the venue for their wedding. The defendant has acknowledged service but the deadline for service of the defence will be impossible for them to meet. There are 18 days left and the claimants have refused to agree any extension of time. What is the correct procedure for the defendant to ext defence?
subject: Dispute Resolution
correctAnswer: Issue and serve an application for an order to ext a witness statement explaining the reason further time is needed.

questionText: A defendant is charged with murder of a victim as an accessory to a second defendant. There is evidence that the first defendant had suggested that the second kill the victim and that the first defendant wanted the victim dead but they have produced evidence that the second defendant had been talking about doing so anyway. Can the first defendant be an accessory to murder of the victim on this basis?
subject: Criminal Liability
source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)
userAnswer: Yes, if what the first defendant said made a difference to whether the second defendant would actually kill the victim and the first defendant realised it might do so.
correctAnswer: Yes, if the first defendant intended to encourage the second to kill the victim and knew that what was said might do so.

questionText: A defendant is on trial for the murder of their parent. The defence is diminished responsibility. The defendant has produced evidence to show that a history of poor treatment substantially impaired their capacity to make rational judgements. The jurors retired to consider the case but have returned to ask what should happen if they think it unlikely that the defendant’s capacity for rational judgement was substantially impaired but cannot be sure that it was not so impaired. How should the judge direct the jury about when they should conclude that diminished responsibility is established?
subject: Criminal Law and Practice
source: CRMP9.6_ Evidence and proof_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)
userAnswer: They should find diminished responsibility unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant’s capacity was not substantially impaired.
correctAnswer: They should only find diminished responsibility if they conclude it was likely that the defendant’s capacity was substantially impaired.

questionText: A testator has named their spouse, their 70-year-old uncle, and their 10- year-old child as the executors of their estate. Amongst the property being left in the will is the copyright of the testator’s books. Two years before the testator’s death, they and their spouse divorced. The testator executed a codicil to their will to confirm that their spouse would remain an executor to their will. Seven years after the execution of their will, the testator and their uncle were in a car accident, both dying at the scene. Which of the following statements accurately addresses the issue of the appointed executors to the will?
subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
source: WILL13.3_ Personal representatives and interpretations of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)
userAnswer: A testator must have at least two executors for their will. As neither the daughter nor the uncle can fulfil this role, there will not be sufficient executors to administer the will.
correctAnswer: The testator’s spouse can be an executor because the testator has demonstrated their intention for their former spouse to retain this role, despite their divorce.

questionText: A settlor wants to create a trust over £500,000 to benefit their descendants equally. Which of the following best describes this trust?
subject: Trusts Law
userAnswer: This is a fixed trust for a class of objects which will require the trustees to identify all potential beneficiaries by applying the any given postulant test.
correctAnswer: This is a fixed trust for a class of objects which will require the trustees to identify all potential beneficiaries and establish conceptual certainty of the class of descendants.

questionText: A solicitor has been sued for professional negligence in relation to advice concerning a corporate transaction. It is alleged that, due to the negligent advice, an important element of the transaction was ineffective, causing substantial losses. The solicitor denies negligence, saying the client gave incorrect instructions. Alternatively, the solicitor claims the client was contributorily negligent because they did not read the assumptions contained in the advice before proceeding with the transaction. Which party bears the burden of proof concerning the alleged negligence of the solicitor?
subject: Dispute Resolution
userAnswer: The solicitor, because they allege a positive case of contributory negligence.
correctAnswer: The client, because as claimant they bear the burden of proof on their case.

questionText: A solicitor recently acted for an existing client in the purchase of property. The client had previously deposited two significant cheques into the firm’s client bank account on an alleged purchase of a new development site to cover the deposit and legal fees for the transaction. On both occasions, after 2 weeks, the client instructed that the development has fallen through, and so will not proceed any further and instructed the firm to return the money, less an amount for its fees. On completion of the recent purchase, the client instructs the solicitor to transfer the house to a relative of the client. What should the solicitor do?
subject: Legal Services
userAnswer: The solicitor will not be committing any offence under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 as the solicitor has no actual knowledge that the property was purchased with the proceeds of crime.
correctAnswer: The solicitor will commit an offence under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 if they act on the client’s instructions.

questionText: A solicitor acts for a client in relation to the acquisition of a private limited company. Two days before the transaction is due to complete, the solicitor suspects that the client will be using the transaction to launder money. The solicitor reports this to the nominated officer who makes a suspicious activity report to the relevant authority. What action should the solicitor now take?
subject: Legal Services
userAnswer: Proceed with the transaction after a period of 3 days if no response is received from the relevant authority.
correctAnswer: Proceed with the transaction only after receiving authorisation from the relevant authority.

questionText: A department store ordered boxed chocolates to sell in its store. It was listed as a written term of the contract that the chocolates be packaged in the store’s own-brand packaging, as the store famously only sells own- branded products. Once delivered it was discovered that the chocolates were instead in packaging representing the manufacturer’s brand. The manufacturer claims the packaging detail was only a warranty and the store can still sell the goods. The department store says it was obviously a condition and they cannot sell the goods. What is the likely legal position?
subject: Contract Law
userAnswer: The clause was an innominate term, the breach of which amounts to a breach of a condition as it deprives the department store of the “substantial benefit” of the contract.
correctAnswer: The clause will be held to be a condition of the contract.

questionText: A person has been arrested and detained on suspicion of criminal damage by daubing a £1,000 political advertising board with red paint (a summary offence). A police officer saw the person commit the offence and arrested them immediately. The person wishes to receive legal advice but a superintendent at the station has authorised a delay of legal advice on the basis that they have reasonable grounds for suspecting that exercising the right to legal advice will interfere with evidence. The detainee subsequently confesses during their Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 interview. The admissibility of the confession is challenged at trial. Which of the following is the best argument for the defence to exclude the confession?
subject: Criminal Law and Practice
source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: The requirement is that the superintendent must have reasonable grounds for believing, not merely suspecting, that exercising the right to legal advice will interfere with evidence.
correctAnswer: This offence was summary only so there was no basis for preventing legal advice.

questionText: The Law Society has produced a statement of best practice for conveyancing. It contains a set of steps to follow when acting in the sale and/or purchase of a home for an owner occupier. What is this statement of best practice called?
subject: Property Law and Practice
source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: The Formulae for Exchange
correctAnswer: The Law Society Conveyancing Protocol

questionText: A person has died and under the will appoints their neighbour as personal representative. The will states that everything must be divided equally between their nieces. The personal representative knows of only two living nieces and contacts them both. Several months after the estate is settled another niece comes forward seeking their share of the will. Would the neighbour be personally liable to the unpaid beneficiary?
subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
userAnswer: Personal representatives are not personally liable to any unpaid beneficiary if it is not known when a distribution is made.
correctAnswer: Personal representatives are personally liable to any unpaid beneficiary, even if it is not known when a distribution is made, unless they comply with s 27 of the Trustee Act 1925.

questionText: During a rally, the defendant fires off a gun. The shot shatters a window and narrowly misses a person standing beyond it. The defendant denies having intended to put anyone’s life at risk claiming instead simply to have been joining in the spirit of the protest. Could the defendant be guilty of aggravated criminal damage?
subject: Criminal Liability
userAnswer: Yes, if the defendant realised that firing the bullet through the window put the person in danger.
correctAnswer: No, because there does not appear to be any recklessness as to endangering life by damage to property.

questionText: A solicitor in an SRA-regulated firm is having an extra-marital relationship. The solicitor wishes to marry their new lover but is too embarrassed to go through a divorce. The solicitor travels to another part of the country and goes through a ceremony of marriage with the new lover, without the knowledge of their first spouse. The deception is later discovered by the first spouse, who reports the matter to the police. The solicitor is convicted of bigamy and sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications of the solicitor’s actions?
subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
source: COND3.2_ Overview of Principles and Codes Part 2
userAnswer: The solicitor has breached the conduct regulations in light of the fact that a criminal offence has been committed.
correctAnswer: The solicitor has breached the professional conduct regulations as they have acted dishonestly.

questionText: The defendant is charged with burglary. At the trial in the Crown Court, officers give evidence to the effect that, upon their arrival at the burgled house, they noticed that the kitchen glass window had been smashed and then saw the defendant hiding down a rear alleyway close to the burgled. The defendant was breathing heavily, sweating profusely and his trousers had a jagged tear. The evidence from the police officers at the scene is that they reasonably believed that the tear was a result of the defendant’s commission of the burglary. They also said that, in interview, after the standard caution about the right to silence, they had told the defendant of their belief that the defendant was down the alleyway because they had committed the offence and asked the defendant to account for his presence at the scene but the defendant refused to tell them. No other caution was administered. May the court draw such inferences as appear proper from the defendant’s refusal to account for the condition of their clothing?
subject: Criminal Law and Practice
source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
userAnswer: No, because such inferences can only be drawn from failure or refusal to account for presence at the scene.
correctAnswer: No, the court may not draw inferences from the refusal to account for the condition of their clothing.

questionText: A couple are purchasing a property and have instructed a solicitor who notes from the Property Information Form that the seller built a garage at the property 8 years ago. The solicitor has received the local search result which reveals that the property is not listed and that no planning permissions relating to this property. Should the buyers be concerned about the lack of planning permission?
subject: Property Law and Practice
source: PROP12.6_ Core principles of planning law_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)
userAnswer: Yes, because the local authority has unlimited jurisdiction to take enforcement action for lack of planning permission.
correctAnswer: No, because the time limit for enforcement action for lack of planning permission passed 4 years ago.

questionText: A solicitor has exchanged contracts for a company client on the purchase of a commercial unit with a registered title. Completion is not due to take place for another 3 months. What should the solicitor do to protect their client’s contract?
subject: Property Law and Practice
userAnswer: Advise their client to put the buildings insurance on risk.
correctAnswer: Register a notice on the seller’s title at HM Land Registry.

questionText: Three business partners run a firm of financial advisers as a general partnership. Two of the partners are in dispute with a parent of the other partner, who has received a substantial amount of financial advice and agreed to pay commercial terms. However, the parent is now unwilling to pay. The two partners intend to commence a claim against the third partner’s parent for unpaid bills, rendered over the last 3 years, in the sum of £25,000 plus interest. The two partners are individual claimants. The third business partner does not want to participate in the claim against their parent. Which of the following statements best describes how or if the proceedings should progress?
subject: Dispute Resolution
userAnswer: The third business partner should be added as a claimant.
correctAnswer: The third business partner should be added as a defendant.

questionText: A solicitor is instructed on the purchase of company shares. The solicitor discovers that a colleague in the firm has been instructed by the same client in respect of an investigation by the Italian tax authorities into certain of the client’s business activities in Italy, which are alleged to amount to tax fraud. The solicitor makes an authorised disclosure to the firm’s nominated officer. The nominated officer does not go on to make a suspicious activity report to the National Crime Agency. Forty-eight hours later, having heard nothing from the nominated officer, the solicitor buys the shares on the client’s behalf. Is the solicitor likely to have committed the offence of “arranging” under Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 s 328?
subject: Legal Services
userAnswer: Yes, because a suspicious activity report has not been made to the National Crime Agency.
correctAnswer: Yes because the solicitor did not have appropriate consent to proceed with the purchase of the shares.

questionText: A shareholder is the sole owner of a company. They also own a piece of land. They require some building work to be done on the land, and their company entered into a contract with a builder to carry out some work on the land. The company failed to pay the builder and the builder tried to claim payment from the shareholder on the basis of unjust enrichment. Can the builder succeed?
subject: Contract Law
userAnswer: Yes, because the work had improved the value of the land.
correctAnswer: No, because the shareholder was not party to the contract.

questionText: A solicitor is the executor of a person’s estate. The person died 3 months ago leaving their estate equally between a friend and their sibling. The friend went to Australia, and so far, attempts to trace them have failed. The executor has placed advertisements for claimants to the estate in the appropriate newspapers and waited 2 months. The executor has now paid all the debts of which they have knowledge. The person had an illegitimate child (aged 40) who is complaining that they should have been left something but so far has taken no legal steps to make a claim. The sibling wants the executor to distribute the entire estate to them. If the executor distributes the estate to the sister having waited 2 months, which of the following correctly states the protection offered by the advertisements?
subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
userAnswer: The advertisements will protect the executor from liability to the friend but not to the daughter.
correctAnswer: The advertisements will not protect the executor from liability to either the friend or the daughter.

questionText: A person dies. The deceased’s will leaves their house (value £1m) to their sibling’s eldest child and their shares in a private company (value £1m) to their sibling’s second child. There is a pecuniary legacy of £1m to the deceased’s sibling. The deceased leaves the residue of their estate (value approximately £1m) to be divided equally between a named charity and their godchild. The deceased’s godchild dies before the deceased. The deceased is survived by their sibling’s two children and their sibling. There are unsecured debts of £20,000 to pay and a mortgage of £100,000 secured on the house. The will contains no directions as to the payment of debts or the payment of the mortgage Which of the following statements correctly sets out the legal position relating to the order in which assets will be taken to pay debts?
subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
userAnswer: The debts, including the mortgage, will be paid from the residue of the estate before it is divided into shares.
correctAnswer: The debts, excluding the mortgage, will be paid from the lapsed share of residue.

questionText: A person has died leaving an investment property to their first child, shares worth £100,000 to their second child and a legacy of £100,000 to their sibling’s child. The residue of their estate is left to their spouse. The first child (who is divorced) would like to pass the investment property to their only child but does not want to make a transfer of value for inheritance tax purposes or a disposal for capital gains tax purposes. They have already received rent from the property. The second child does not want the shares and wants their parent to have them. They have refused all dividends. Like their sibling, they do not want to make a transfer of value or a disposal. The child of the person’s sibling would like to give £50,000 of their legacy to their sibling. Like the person’s first child, they do not want to make a transfer of value or a disposal. Which of the following correctly states a method by which one of the beneficiaries can achieve their desired result?
subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
userAnswer: If the second child disclaims their entitlement to the shares in writing, they will pass automatically to their mother, but they must include a statement of intent that there is to be no transfer of value or disposal.
correctAnswer: The child of the person’s sibling can vary the terms of the will in writing to give £50,000 to their sibling but they must include a statement of intent that there is to be no transfer of value or disposal.

questionText: The defendant has been charged with aggravated burglary. The defendant was invited into the victim’s flat to agree a payment of the defendant for work they have done as a drug courier. The two argued and the defendant decided to take all the money the victim had. The defendant pulled out a knife to stop the victim from resisting and ran off with the money. What offence most accurately reflects what the defendant has done on these facts?
subject: Criminal Liability

questionText: A defendant is on trial for theft for finding used car parking tickets with time still to run on them and selling them to new users of the car park. userAnswer: They should determine whether selling the tickets was objectively dishonest and, if so, whether the defendant understood it to be dishonest.

questionText: Defendant A has been charged with causing grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent to cause GBH on a victim and Defendant B is charged as an accessory. questionText: The defendant has been charged with theft from their neighbour. The defendant was paid an amount of cash to invest in Company A on behalf of the neighbour. questionText: Two former business partners are in dispute concerning the allocation of money between them following the dissolution of their partnership. correctAnswer: The third business partner should be added as a defendant.

questionText: A taxi driver who lives and works in Torquay has been sued by the company for which they work for allegedly underreporting fares. correctAnswer: Both within 28 days of the date of deemed service of the particulars of claim.

questionText: An experienced solicitor in a firm specialising in family law is advising a client who has just obtained a substantial settlement in a divorce. questionText: A private limited company is to be incorporated with two classes of shares, A shares and B shares. questionText: A negligence claim has been brought against a small firm of architects in relation to a building project they designed for the claimant 4 years ago. questionText: A seller and a first-time buyer exchanged contracts for the sale of the th seller’s residential property using the Standard Conditions of Sale (5 edition – 2018 revision) (the Standard Conditions) unamended.
